work.title: Work
work.body: I'm a software engineer with a decade of experience across a wide variety of industries and architectural concerns. My software supports robotics, financial transactions, animations across the internet, and skyscraper construction.

life.title: Life
life.body: In addition to software, I stay active with my hobbies and my family: fly fishing, cloud architecture, wine, and my dogs. My wife and I love to travel--Colorado holds a special place in our hearts.

study.title: Study
study.body: Formal education in music: I received a doctorate (DMA) from UT Austin, where my research was in performance psychology as it applied to vocal pedagogy. Also a proud alumnus of the University of Cincinnati, and Baylor University.

NeuralNet.startNote: This downloads TensorFlow.js and trains a network on your device, which can be heavy on slower machines.
NeuralNet.title: Neural Net Playground
NeuralNet.intro: A tiny neural network learning to separate red from blue, live in your browser with TensorFlow.js. Watch the colored boundary bend as it trains.
NeuralNet.canvasLabel: Training data and decision boundary. Press arrow keys to move a cursor and Enter to add a {brush} point.
NeuralNet.canvasHint: Click or tap to add a point of the selected class, or use the arrow keys and Enter. The model keeps training on your points.
NeuralNet.loadError: TensorFlow.js could not be loaded in this browser.
NeuralNet.whatIsTensor: A tensor is just a grid of numbers with a shape. Here, the points are a [N, 2] tensor (one row of x, y per point) and their colors are a [N, 1] tensor. The background is one pass of the network over a [2500, 2] tensor of grid coordinates, all at once. Each layer's weights are variables, the one kind of tensor that can change, which is how training happens.
NeuralNet.memoryNote: Browser gotcha: tensors live in GPU memory and aren't garbage collected. Per-frame work is wrapped in tf.tidy(), and models are dispose()d on reset or when you leave the page. Watch “Live tensors” stay flat while it trains.

Boids.title: Rust Boids
Boids.intro: Three simulations powered by Rust compiled to WebAssembly: a flock, a flock hunted by predators, and slime-mold trails. Pick one, tune its rules, press to interact, and switch to the JavaScript port to see what the speedup is worth.
Boids.loadError: WebAssembly could not be loaded in this browser.
Boids.howItWorks: Each boid follows three rules: steer away from close neighbors (separation), match the heading of nearby ones (alignment), and drift toward their center (cohesion). Flocking emerges from nothing else. To avoid comparing every boid with every other, they are sorted into a grid each frame so only the 3×3 surrounding cells are checked.
Boids.whyWasm: The simulation is a few hundred lines of dependency-free Rust. JavaScript never copies boid data: it reads x, y and velocity straight out of WebAssembly's linear memory and draws them. The JavaScript engine is a line-for-line port of the same algorithm, so “Step time” compares like with like. Try 16,000 boids on each.

canvasLabels.flock: A flock of small triangles moving and turning together.
canvasLabels.predators: A flock of small triangles fleeing from a few larger predator triangles that chase and catch them.
canvasLabels.slime: Glowing trails left by thousands of agents, forming a branching network.

hints.flock: Press and hold on the flock to pull it toward you and turn it green, or hold Shift while pressing to scare it away.
hints.predators: Predators hunt the nearest boid, and the flock scatters from them. Press and hold to pull the flock in, or hold Shift to scare it.
hints.slime: Press and hold to lay down scent that the slime follows, or hold Shift while pressing to wipe it away.

Boids.predatorNote: In Predators mode each hunter chases the nearest boid and rests for a moment after a catch. Boids nearby panic: they steer away and can sprint a third faster than their normal top speed. A caught boid respawns somewhere else, so the flock never runs out.
Boids.slimeNote: Slime mode is a different simulation in the same Rust module. Each agent senses the trail ahead, to the left and to the right, turns toward the strongest scent, and leaves scent behind. The trail is blurred and fades every frame, and from those few rules a branching network emerges, much like the slime mold Physarum.

Signature.title: Cursive Signature
Signature.intro: My name, written out in cursive two ways: by Rust compiled to WebAssembly, and by a Lottie animation played with lottie-react. Switch between them.
Signature.label: The name Chance Eakin being written out in cursive, letter by letter.
Signature.howItWorks: Each letter is a set of bezier outlines, baked into the module from an open-licensed script font. Rust flattens them into polylines once and measures their lengths. For any moment in the animation it returns the first part of each outline, which is what a Trim Paths animation does in After Effects, plus how far the fill has faded in. The page reads those points straight out of WebAssembly's memory and draws them on a canvas.
Signature.swapIt: The Rust engine has no animation file: its timing is a few constants in the Rust source (about 200 lines, no dependencies). The Lottie engine plays a JSON file of shape layers with Trim Paths, the same structure Bodymovin exports from After Effects, so a hand-animated export can replace it. Both come from the same outlines, generated from an open-licensed script font by a script in the repo. Both follow the site theme, and with reduced motion on they show the finished name instead of writing it.

Water.title: Water Sphere
Water.intro: A swirling ball of water made of thousands of droplets, simulated and projected in 3D by Rust compiled to WebAssembly. Click it and it sprays apart, then pours back together. Drag to look around it.
Water.loadError: WebAssembly could not be loaded in this browser.
Water.canvasLabel: A glassy green-and-mustard sphere of water droplets swirling in ribbons. Clicking it sprays the droplets apart, and they then flow back together.
Water.hint: Click the water to splash it apart. Drag to turn the camera around the sphere.
Water.howItWorks: Every droplet has a home on a sphere: most sit in six helical ribbons, the rest fill the body. A spring pulls each droplet toward its home while the whole sphere turns and the ribbons wind and unwind, and that is all the swirling is. Light from the upper left shades each droplet by which way its patch of water faces.
Water.splashNote: A click casts a ray through the sphere and kicks every droplet outward, hardest near where you hit it, with a twist added. The springs switch off, so the droplets fly free under light drag and gravity, and the fastest stretch into streaks. Then each one's spring eases back in at its own moment, with a sideways sweep so they spiral home instead of falling straight back.
Water.whyWasm: Rust does all of it: the physics, the orbit camera, the perspective projection and a counting sort that orders every droplet from far to near. JavaScript only reads the finished draw list out of WebAssembly's memory and paints glass-bubble sprites onto a 2D canvas, so there is no WebGL and no copying of droplet data. The module is about 300 lines with no dependencies.
